blocks.content: A user logs in once. Then, on every request after that, your server needs to answer one question instantly: is this really them, and are they allowed to do this? A JWT is one of the most popular ways to answer that question at scale, without the server having to remember anyone.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520726-352517105.png

JWT, short for JSON Web Token, is a compact, signed piece of data that a client carries with every request to prove who it is. It shows up in almost every modern system design, so it is worth understanding deeply, not just using blindly.

In this lesson we open a JWT up completely: what it is made of, how the signature makes it trustworthy, how the full login flow works, why it lets your system stay stateless, and the security mistakes that get people breached. We keep it visual and practical throughout.
1. What a JWT Actually Is

A JWT is a small, self contained token that carries information about a user, and is signed so it cannot be tampered with. When a user logs in, the server hands them a token. From then on, the client sends that token with every request, and the server trusts it after checking the signature.

The key idea hides in the words self contained. The token itself carries the facts about the user, such as their id and role. The server does not need to look anything up to know who is calling. That single property is what makes JWT so powerful for large systems.

blocks.title: The one line definition
blocks.content: A JWT is a signed JSON object that proves a claim, such as "I am user 42 and I am an admin", without the server needing to store or look up anything.
A JWT is usually sent in the HTTP Authorization header, like this:

GET /api/orders
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiJ9.s5T...
That long string is the token. Let us take it apart.
2. The Three Parts of a Token
blocks.text: 2. The Three Parts of a Token

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277746437-433987775.png
blocks.alt: A JWT has three parts: header, payload, signature

blocks.content: A JWT is three pieces of text joined by dots: header, payload, and signature. It always looks like this:

xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz
header.payload.signature

Each of the first two parts is just a JSON object that has been Base64 encoded, which turns it into a URL safe string. The third part, the signature, is what proves the token is genuine. We will look at each part in turn.

blocks.title: Base64 is not encryption
blocks.content: Anyone can decode the header and payload of a JWT and read them. Base64 only makes the JSON compact and URL safe, it does not hide anything. Never put secrets in a JWT payload.
3. The Header
The header is a tiny JSON object that describes the token itself: what type it is, and which algorithm signs it.
["alg: the signing algorithm, such as HS256 or RS256.","typ: the token type, which is simply JWT."]
items: alg: the signing algorithm, such as HS256 or RS256.
typ: the token type, which is simply JWT.

blocks.content: The server reads the header to know how to verify the signature. This part is small and rarely changes.
4. The Payload and Its Claims
The payload is the heart of the token. It holds the claims, which are statements about the user and the token itself.
Standard claims

{"headers":["Claim","Meaning"],"rows":[["sub","Subject, usually the user id"],["iat","Issued at, when the token was created"],["exp","Expiry, when the token stops being valid"],["iss","Issuer, who created the token"],["aud","Audience, who the token is for"]]}
Custom claims
You can add your own claims too, like a role or a plan. Keep the payload small, because it travels on every single request. And remember: it is readable, so never put passwords or secrets in it.

blocks.title: Keep it lean
blocks.content: Every extra claim adds weight to every request. Put the few things you truly need, like the user id and role, and look up the rest from your database when required.
5. The Signature
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277748012-364113638.png
blocks.alt: How the server verifies a JWT signature

blocks.content: The signature is what makes a JWT trustworthy. Without it, anyone could edit the payload and claim to be an admin. The signature stops that cold.
The server creates the signature by taking the header and payload, and running them through the signing algorithm together with a secret key that only the server knows.

signature = HMAC_SHA256(
    base64(header) + "." + base64(payload),
    secretKey
)

Because the secret is known only to the server, only the server can produce a valid signature. If an attacker changes even one character of the payload, the signature no longer matches, and the server rejects the token instantly.
The payload is readable by anyone, but it is not changeable by anyone. The signature is the seal that proves nobody has tampered with it.
6. How JWT Authentication Works
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277749730-203390482.png
Now let us put it together into the full flow, the part interviewers love to see you draw.

["The user logs in with their username and password.","The server verifies the credentials, then creates a JWT and signs it with its secret.","The server sends the token back to the client.","The client stores the token and attaches it to every future request in the Authorization header.","On each request, the server checks the signature and expiry, and if valid, trusts the claims and serves the request."]
items: The user logs in with their username and password.
The server verifies the credentials, then creates a JWT and signs it with its secret.
The server sends the token back to the client.
The client stores the token and attaches it to every future request in the Authorization header.
On each request, the server checks the signature and expiry, and if valid, trusts the claims and serves the request.

blocks.content: Notice step five carefully. The server does not look the user up in any session store. It simply re verifies the signature of the token the client sent. That is the whole trick, and it is what we explore next.
7. Why JWT Is Stateless
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521154-835244941.png
blocks.alt: Session based stores state, JWT is stateless

blocks.content: In older session based authentication, the server stores a session for every logged in user, and looks it up on every request. That store becomes a bottleneck and a scaling headache, especially across many servers.

JWT flips this around. The proof lives in the token, carried by the client, not on the server. The server keeps no session record at all. To check a request, it only needs its secret key and a little maths.

["Any server with the secret can verify any token, so you can add servers freely.","There is no shared session store to become a single point of failure.","Scaling out is easy, because servers share nothing about logged in users."]
items: Any server with the secret can verify any token, so you can add servers freely.
There is no shared session store to become a single point of failure.
Scaling out is easy, because servers share nothing about logged in users.

blocks.title: The tradeoff of statelessness
blocks.content: Because nothing is stored, you cannot easily revoke a single JWT before it expires. This is the classic JWT tradeoff, and refresh tokens plus short lifetimes are how systems manage it.
8. Access Tokens and Refresh Tokens
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521154-3142066.png
blocks.alt: Access and refresh tokens working together

blocks.content: If a token is stolen, you want the damage window to be small. So real systems use two tokens working together.

{"headers":["Token","Lifetime","Job"],"rows":[["Access token","Short, minutes","Sent on every request to prove identity"],["Refresh token","Long, days or weeks","Used only to get a new access token"]]}

The short lived access token does the everyday work. When it expires, the client quietly uses the refresh token to get a fresh access token, without asking the user to log in again. If an access token is stolen, it dies quickly on its own.
The refresh token is more sensitive and is stored more carefully, often in a secure cookie, and it can be revoked on the server if needed.
9. Verifying a Token
Every time a request arrives, the server runs a quick set of checks before trusting the token.

["Recompute the signature from the header and payload using the secret, and confirm it matches.","Check the expiry claim, and reject the token if it has passed.","Optionally check the issuer and audience claims.","Only then, trust the claims and let the request through."]
items: Recompute the signature from the header and payload using the secret, and confirm it matches.
Check the expiry claim, and reject the token if it has passed.
Optionally check the issuer and audience claims.
Only then, trust the claims and let the request through.

blocks.content: This is fast, needs no database, and can happen on any server. That speed is a big reason JWT is so popular.
10. Signing Algorithms
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521155-455879644.png
blocks.alt: HMAC uses one shared secret, RSA uses a key pair

blocks.content: There are two families of signing algorithms, and the choice matters for how your system is shaped.
Symmetric: HMAC (HS256)
One secret key both signs and verifies. It is simple and fast, but every service that verifies tokens must hold the same secret. Good when one trusted service issues and verifies.
Asymmetric: RSA or ECDSA (RS256)

A private key signs, and a separate public key verifies. Only the auth server holds the private key, while any number of services can verify using the freely shareable public key. This is safer for larger systems with many services.

{"headers":["Aspect","HMAC (HS256)","RSA (RS256)"],"rows":[["Keys","One shared secret","Private plus public key"],["Who can verify","Anyone with the secret","Anyone with the public key"],["Best for","A single trusted service","Many services, one issuer"]]}
11. Where to Store the Token
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521156-393886336.png
blocks.alt: Local storage risks XSS, httpOnly cookie is safer

blocks.content: On the client, where you keep the token decides which attacks you are exposed to. There is no perfect spot, only tradeoffs.
Local storage

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Simple to use from JavaScript","Readable by any script, so a cross site scripting flaw can steal it"],["Easy to attach to requests","Not sent automatically, you must add it yourself"]]}
An httpOnly cookie

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Not readable by JavaScript, so it survives cross site scripting","Can be exposed to cross site request forgery, so needs protection"],["Sent automatically by the browser","A little more setup"]]}

blocks.title: The usual advice
blocks.content: For most web apps, store the token in an httpOnly, secure cookie and add cross site request forgery protection. It defends against the more common and more damaging script based theft.
12. Common Security Mistakes
JWT is safe only when used carefully. These mistakes cause real breaches.

["Putting secrets in the payload: it is readable by anyone, so never store passwords or private data there.","No expiry: a token that never expires is a permanent key if stolen. Always set a short exp.","Accepting the none algorithm: some libraries once allowed an unsigned token if alg was set to none. Always reject it.","A weak secret: a short, guessable secret can be brute forced. Use a long, random one.","A giant payload: it travels on every request, so keep it small.","No way to revoke: plan for logout and stolen tokens with short lifetimes and refresh tokens."]
items: Putting secrets in the payload: it is readable by anyone, so never store passwords or private data there.
No expiry: a token that never expires is a permanent key if stolen. Always set a short exp.
Accepting the none algorithm: some libraries once allowed an unsigned token if alg was set to none. Always reject it.
A weak secret: a short, guessable secret can be brute forced. Use a long, random one.
A giant payload: it travels on every request, so keep it small.
No way to revoke: plan for logout and stolen tokens with short lifetimes and refresh tokens.

blocks.content: A JWT is only as trustworthy as the secret that signs it and the discipline with which it is used. Treat the secret like a crown jewel.
13. When to Use JWT
JWT is a great fit for many systems, but not all. Choose it on purpose.

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Stateless services that must scale horizontally","You need to revoke individual sessions instantly"],["APIs consumed by mobile apps and other services","A simple single server app where sessions are easier"],["Single sign on and sharing identity across services","You would store large or changing data in the token"],["Short lived, self contained access tokens",""]]}

blocks.title: A balanced view
blocks.content: JWT shines for stateless, distributed systems. For a small single server app, plain server sessions are often simpler and let you revoke instantly. Match the tool to the system.
14. JWT in a System Design Interview
blocks.text: 14. JWT in a System Design Interview

blocks.content: When authentication comes up in a design interview, a clear JWT explanation scores well. Here is a calm way to present it.

["State the goal: authenticate every request without a shared session store.","Describe the flow: log in, issue a signed token, client sends it, server verifies the signature.","Explain statelessness and why it scales across many servers.","Mention access plus refresh tokens for security and revocation.","Call out the tradeoff: hard to revoke a single token, solved with short lifetimes."]
items: State the goal: authenticate every request without a shared session store.
Describe the flow: log in, issue a signed token, client sends it, server verifies the signature.
Explain statelessness and why it scales across many servers.
Mention access plus refresh tokens for security and revocation.
Call out the tradeoff: hard to revoke a single token, solved with short lifetimes.

blocks.title: The line that impresses
blocks.content: Saying "JWT trades easy revocation for statelessness, so I use short lived access tokens with refresh tokens to get both scale and safety" shows real depth.
15. Common Questions
Is a JWT encrypted? - No, by default it is only signed, not encrypted. Anyone can read the payload. It is protected from tampering, not from reading. Do not put secrets in it.
Can I revoke a JWT? - Not easily, because the server stores nothing. You use short lifetimes, refresh tokens, or a small blocklist of revoked tokens as a workaround.
Where should the token live on the client? - For web apps, an httpOnly secure cookie is usually safest against script based theft, paired with cross site request forgery protection.
HMAC or RSA? - Use HMAC when one trusted service issues and verifies. Use RSA when many services must verify tokens issued by one auth server.
What happens when a token expires? - The server rejects it. The client then uses its refresh token to get a new access token, so the user is not forced to log in again.
16. Key Takeaways

["A JWT is a signed, self contained token that proves who a user is.","It has three parts: header, payload, and signature, joined by dots.","The payload is readable, so it holds no secrets, and the signature stops tampering.","JWT is stateless, so any server with the secret can verify any token, which scales beautifully.","Use short lived access tokens with longer refresh tokens for safety.","Its main tradeoff is that individual tokens are hard to revoke.","Guard the signing secret, always set an expiry, and never trust the none algorithm."]
items: A JWT is a signed, self contained token that proves who a user is.
It has three parts: header, payload, and signature, joined by dots.
The payload is readable, so it holds no secrets, and the signature stops tampering.
JWT is stateless, so any server with the secret can verify any token, which scales beautifully.
Use short lived access tokens with longer refresh tokens for safety.
Its main tradeoff is that individual tokens are hard to revoke.
Guard the signing secret, always set an expiry, and never trust the none algorithm.

blocks.content: Understand these pieces and you can confidently design, explain, and secure authentication in almost any modern system. JWT is small on the wire but big in what it enables.
